profiles.name: Margaret Butler
profiles.description: Margaret Butler, born in Portland in 1957, was a Communications Workers of America activist who co-founded Portland Jobs with Justice in 1991 and later directed the coalition. During its 1993 National Day of Action for Labor Law Reform sit-in at the National Labor Relations Board offices, she was one of nine people arrested when police cleared the lobby. The accessible oral history does not give the exact arrest date, booking details, disposition or any period of confinement.
profiles.finding: Verified captioned Northwest Labor Press portrait; CWA and OHS independently confirm identity. Original200x320 preserved, deployed photo-only after strict snapshot guard; public profile and asset HTTP200 and screenshot confirm recognizable undistorted image.
profiles.rights: Copyright Northwest Labor Press; photographer unidentified, no open license stated. See batch97.json.

profiles.name: Ana Lucia Gelabert
profiles.description: Ana Lucia Gelabert was born in central Cuba on July 6, 1938 and returned to the United States in 1961. On December 26, 1983, Houston police responded after Gelabert threatened suicide during a family dispute. She fired toward arriving officers, later testifying that she hoped they would kill her; Gelabert and one officer were wounded. A jury convicted her on two counts of attempted capital murder of a police officer and imposed concurrent life sentences. In prison she became a leader of Prisoners United for Revolutionary Education, wrote on international politics and prison conditions, helped organize a women’s hunger strike against a scheduled execution, and created the political comic series “Connie Convicta and Vato Emiliano.” She died in prison in 2013.
profiles.finding: Real Cost of Prisons confirms artist and death2013; comics explicitly copyrighted, not portrait evidence. No verified real portrait found.

profiles.name: Carl Johnson
profiles.description: Carl Edward Johnson was an internet forum participant in the cypherpunk community who circulated messages associated with the “Assassination Politics” concept. Federal prosecutors charged him over messages naming a magistrate judge, a federal appellate judge, Internal Revenue Service personnel, and Bill Gates. A federal judge convicted him on four counts in April 1999. He received 37 months in federal custody with credit for time served, followed by three years of supervised release.

profiles.name: Elizabeth Walz
profiles.description:
Elizabeth Walz is associated with Christian pacifist direct action and the Plowshares movement tradition of symbolic “disarmament” actions. She was part of a small group that physically entered a military aviation facility as a protest against U.S. war-making capacity, using hammers and blood as deliberately symbolic tools meant to dramatize the human costs of modern weapons.

The action led to arrest and federal prosecution, and Walz received a prison sentence as the courts treated the protest as criminal damage and unlawful entry rather than protected demonstration. Her case is frequently discussed within the broader history of faith-based antiwar resistance in which activists accept arrest and imprisonment as part of a moral witness strategy.

profiles.name: Thomas Warner
profiles.description:
Thomas Warner was identified in prisoner-support and political-prisoner listings as a man associated with the Black Panther Party era of U.S. radical politics. He is typically described in those contexts as a political prisoner held in the Pennsylvania prison system, though detailed public documentation of the specific underlying case is comparatively sparse in widely circulated sources.

What is consistently reported in those listings is that he remained incarcerated for years and died by suicide in prison in 1998. Because granular case facts are not broadly available in mainstream summaries, accounts of Warner’s activism and prosecution tend to be presented in brief memorial form rather than as a fully documented public narrative.
profiles.finding: LA ABC memorial confirms death1998; no real portrait verified.

profiles.name: Kijana Tashiri Askari
profiles.description: Kijana Tashiri Askari, also known as Marcus L. Harrison, is a New Afrikan prison organizer and writer who chaired the W.L. Nolen Mentorship Program. He challenged censorship of Black August and other political correspondence at Pelican Bay. He attributes his prolonged solitary confinement to political commemoration; prison officials relied on gang validation. He later joined the Ashker class action and reported transfer to general population in 2015. Supporters still sought parole assistance in 2021. His present custody status and vital dates remain unverified.

profiles.name: Kevin Mills
profiles.description: Kevin Mills was a 20-year-old Army reservist from Washington, D.C., assigned to the 400th Military Police Battalion at Fort Meade. He left without authorization on February 4, 1991 after his unit was called for Persian Gulf duty. On March 3, after speaking against the war at Union Temple Baptist Church, he surrendered to military authorities at Anacostia Naval Station. The available contemporaneous report does not establish how long authorities held him, what charges followed or the final military disposition.
